newsitem.title: POLAND: U.S.-based body to save fragment of Jewish Warsaw.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-based body to save fragment of Jewish Warsaw.

text.p: A U.S.-based foundation bought a crumbling building in Warsaw on Monday to preserve a last tiny fragment of the once-bustling Jewish quarter levelled when wartime Nazi German invaders murdered its people.
The Jewish Renaissance Foundation said it had acquired 9, Prozna street, near the city's last functioning synagogue, from the Polish capital's central district authorities.

"The...Foundation has undertaken to restore Prozna Street so as to preserve its unique character as an authentic remnant of the centuries-old Polish Jewish culture that was almost entirely destroyed during the Holocaust," the New York-based body said in a statement.

The building is part of a block of four, now dilapidated and supported by scaffolding, which the New York-based body will repair and eventually use for a Jewish bookstore, a shop selling Jewish articles and a kosher bakery and cafe.

The foundation, headed by Ronald Lauder who has already supported various Jewish projects in Warsaw including a school and kindergarten, has acquired rights to the adjoining building at number 7 and will restore the facades of the other two.
It will invest about $7 million in the project, PAP news agency reported foundation officials as saying.
Before World War Two there were 3.5 million Jews in Poland including about one third of the capital's population.

The Nazis penned Warsaw's Jews behind a wall built around much of the Jewish quarter, where huge numbers died of starvation and disease, then took the rest by train to be killed in Treblinka and other extermination camps.

Poorly-armed, starving young Jews launched a desperate uprising in the Nazi-built Ghetto in 1943 and the Nazis sytematically flattened the area to crush a lonely resistance which astonished them by its heroism.

The short Prozna street, registered as a historic monument, survived because it was left outside the Ghetto walls and the tiny block somehow also survived Warsaw's destruction after a city-wide rising against the Germans in 1944.
When the city was rebuilt after the war the former Jewish areas were mostly replaced by stark modern blocks and greenery.
Little but street names recall the busy, narrow overcrowded neighbourhoods, full of small businesses, where Jewish cultural and intellectual life once flourished.
After the Holocaust and waves of post-war emigration there are only about 3,500 practising Jews left in Poland.

The foundation, which plans to recreate Prozna with details and street furniture it had in the 19th century, says the project will not make a profit and is intended to provide a centre for tourists and for local cultural activities.

"Our goal is to create anew an authentic Jewish atmosphere in Warsaw, which was one of the most important centres of European Jewry before the Holocaust," the statement quoted the project's coordinator, lawyer Menachem Rosensaft, as saying.
